title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
authors: Nan Chen, Soledad Villar, Soufiane Hayou
abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.

infographic.key_insight: TipSweep transfers learning rates across trainable transformer block counts using precision-dependent scaling: approximately k⁻¹ with FP32 master weights and k⁻¹ᐟ² with direct BF16 updates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tuning only a small subset of blocks can reduce the memory and compute required to select learning rates for full-model post-training.
method: Search for the best learning rate while training only the last k₀ blocks, typically k₀ = 1.
Predict the learning rate for k trainable blocks by multiplying the tuned rate by (k/k₀)⁻¹ for FP32 master weights or (k/k₀)⁻¹ᐟ² for direct BF16 updates.
Explain the precision-dependent rules with an analytical model accounting for update rounding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments span 1–7B-parameter models; 6.7B-model prototypes fit search on a 16 GiB consumer GPU or evaluate five candidate rates using about half the GPU hours of one full-depth run.
infographic.watch_item: The scaling rules are approximate and depend on update precision; verify whether training uses FP32 master weights or direct BF16 updates before applying them.
infographic.paper_title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training

title: Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks
authors: Burak Demirel, Yu Wang, Pablo Soldati
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation will help future mobile networks translate high-level network intents into concrete network optimization or control actions. However, existing approaches often focus on intent management and orchestration, leaving the adaptation of underlying network optimization and control functions largely unaddressed. This article proposes a triadic agentic AI framework that co-designs intent management and intent fulfillment through three agents: an interpreter, powered by a language model, that translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates; an optimizer that adapts controller policies to intent specifications; and a controller that performs fast decision-making. We discuss the design space of each agent and how the workflow can be embedded across network architectural domains. Finally, we develop a concrete realization combining a language-model interpreter with Bayesian optimization for the optimizer and multi-objective reinforcement learning for the controller, and evaluate it in a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity. Results demonstrate how the agentic AI framework can connect high-level intents with runtime network control, showing adaptability of intent specifications and control policies to service requirements and changing network conditions.

infographic.key_insight: A three-agent AI framework links high-level network intents to adaptive optimization and fast runtime control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help autonomous mobile networks adapt control policies to changing service requirements and network conditions.
method: A language-model interpreter translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates.
A Bayesian optimizer adapts controller policies to intent specifications.
A multi-objective reinforcement-learning controller makes fast network decisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: A radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity demonstrates adaptability, but the abstract reports no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment would require validating intent translations and ensuring policy adaptation preserves network safety and service constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks

title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
authors: Zhengyang Wang, Renfei Tan, Shuze Daniel Liu, David Simchi-Levi
abstract: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-discovered heuristics directly construct promising vehicle-routing subproblems, matching neural selection policies in-distribution and outperforming them on large-scale out-of-distribution instances.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Interpretable, generalizable subproblem construction could help logistics optimization systems tackle large capacitated vehicle routing problems.
method: Use an LLM to autonomously refine subproblem-construction heuristics.
Apply the discovered heuristics to identify promising portions of a large routing problem.
Optimize those subproblems with solvers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparable in-distribution performance and better out-of-distribution performance than neural network-based policies, but gives no numerical results or benchmark sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires validating runtime costs and solution quality on operational routing constraints beyond the evaluated CVRP instances.
infographic.paper_title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing

title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
authors: Anindya Roy Chowdhury, Atanu Barai, Nandakishore Santhi
abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

infographic.key_insight: Randomized orthogonal mixing and progressive residual-sign coding enable training-free Transformer weight compression with fidelity improving as residual stages are added.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers flexible storage–fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization.
method: Orthogonally mix residuals to promote Gaussian-like distributions for sign coding.
Independently normalize and analytically calibrate reconstruction at each residual stage.
Progressively encode residual errors to refine reconstructed weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across attention and MLP projections, five-stage joint quantization achieved perplexities of 32.16 on GPT-2 Large and 12.73 on Llama-3-8B, versus full-precision baselines of 29.89 and 11.07.
infographic.watch_item: Predictive fidelity remains below full precision, and deployment should account for residual-stage storage overhead and runtime trade-offs.
infographic.paper_title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression

title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
authors: Wenlong Yu, Bingxu Lu, Qilong Wang, Qinghua Hu, Qianru Sun
abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

infographic.key_insight: REPA links local agent responses to system-level error propagation, revealing how errors spread through multi-agent LLM workflows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Modeling error propagation can help engineers target recovery interventions rather than rely only on final-answer evaluation.
method: Model error propagation across agents using REPA.
Separately estimate input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels.
Relate local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error through theoretical analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three Qwen base models, six workflows, and ten ErrPropBench-10 settings, REPA achieved mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 versus 0.47 for direct regression; REPA-guided RAG improved accuracy by 19 percentage points over no retrieval with 16% additional tokens.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the tested Qwen models and workflows remains unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
authors: Konstantinos Dovelos
abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

infographic.key_insight: Solver-independent certificates provide guaranteed error bounds for PDE outputs, exposing errors that convergence studies can miss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: An independent checker can verify third-party, LLM-written, and neural solver outputs against specified physics without trusting their implementations.
method: Return an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current as a certificate.
Use a small independent checker to compute guaranteed error bounds.
Apply the same checker to finite-element solvers and neural predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The checker rejected or refuted all five bugs that passed grid-convergence tests, certified one LLM-written solver to 0.1%, and bounded reduced-basis neural predictions with intervals at most 0.0021% wide in-range.
infographic.watch_item: Bounds apply to the stated model, not physical reality, and become informative only with energy-accurate outputs on a sufficiently resolving grid.
infographic.paper_title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates

title: Explanation Selection in Abductive Learning
authors: En-Hao Gao, Yuan Jiang
abstract: Abductive learning (ABL) offers a promising framework that connects machine learning and logical reasoning in a mutually beneficial loop. However, this bidirectional feedback can also reinforce incorrect concept semantics, since different interpretations of intermediate concepts may explain the same observed reasoning outcomes. Static analyses characterize this ambiguity but leave open which explanation training selects and whether its labels can still be corrected. We develop a dynamical analysis of a fixed-feature binary ABL model that links the local stability of competing explanations to differences in their concept labels. We prove that Gram matrices with identical spectra can select different explanations even under the same supervision, objective, and initialization. When any two compatible explanations differ in at least two labels, legal evidence above one half guarantees during training that admissible changes in optimization geometry preserve the selected explanation. Even when only the true explanation satisfies all constraints under a shared predictor, training can still converge to a finite attracting state whose hard predictions violate some constraints and mislabel concepts. Experiments on visual ABL tasks verify these predictions, including wrong attraction from random initializations under identifiable supervision, and show that in ordinary end-to-end training SGD and Adam select different explanations of the same supervision, while unseen concept accuracy drops relative to true-concept references as training concept errors grow.

infographic.key_insight: Abductive learning can reinforce incorrect concept meanings, and optimization geometry can determine which explanation training selects even under identical supervision, objectives, and initialization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Constraint satisfaction alone does not guarantee correct learned concepts, so ABL systems should monitor concept accuracy and sensitivity to optimizer choice.
method: Analyze training dynamics in a fixed-feature binary ABL model.
Link competing explanations’ local stability to differences in their concept labels.
Prove explanation-selection and stability results, then test predictions on visual ABL tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Visual ABL experiments show attraction to incorrect concepts under identifiable supervision, different explanation selection by SGD and Adam, and declining unseen-concept accuracy as training concept errors grow.
infographic.watch_item: The formal guarantees rely on a fixed-feature binary model and specific assumptions; they should not be generalized automatically to end-to-end ABL systems.
infographic.paper_title: Explanation Selection in Abductive Learning

title: TideSand: Performance-Accurate Sandbox Multiplexing for LLM Agents
authors: Shulu Li, Hanchen Li, Xiaokun Chen, Qiuyang Mang, Hanfei Chen, Jacky Kwok
abstract: We propose TideSand, a sandbox system that intelligently multiplexes resources for performance-sensitive LLM agents, such as auto research agents working on system measurement tasks. TideSand combines three key ideas: agent-aware scheduling, which schedules sandbox execution intelligently at the tool call level to avoid resource contention; speculative swapping, which offloads the memory of sandboxes waiting on inference and restores it before their next tool call; and selective rollback, which checkpoints selected sandboxes when contention occurs and restores them when machines are idle. We evaluate TideSand across six model-workload pairs on AlgoTune, Terminal-Bench 4.0, and Terminal-Bench Science. TideSand achieves 3.8-10x higher throughput than strict reservation while maintaining tool-call fidelity, or 7-44% higher fidelity than overcommit baselines at similar throughput. Moreover, TideSand reduces the evaluation error on Algotune by 19x through improved tool-call fidelity. We hope the work motivates future research to maintain tool call fidelity while keeping resource utilization high through statistical multiplexing.

infographic.key_insight: TideSand multiplexes sandbox resources to increase LLM-agent throughput while preserving tool-call fidelity for performance-sensitive tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent infrastructure can improve resource utilization without sacrificing the measurement accuracy needed for automated systems research.
method: Agent-aware scheduling coordinates tool calls to avoid resource contention.
Speculative swapping offloads sandbox memory during inference waits and restores it before the next tool call.
Selective rollback checkpoints chosen sandboxes during contention and restores them when machines are idle.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six model-workload pairs on AlgoTune, Terminal-Bench 4.0, and Terminal-Bench Science, TideSand reports 3.8–10× higher throughput than strict reservation while maintaining fidelity, or 7–44% higher fidelity than overcommit baselines at similar throughput, plus a 19× reduction in AlgoTune evaluation error.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment should validate whether swap and checkpoint overheads remain manageable under different workloads and hardware.
infographic.paper_title: TideSand: Performance-Accurate Sandbox Multiplexing for LLM Agents

title: AlphaDefect: Expert-Level AI for Slay the Spire 2
authors: Qiyue Chen, Taian Yu, Junpei Komiyama, Haobo Huang
abstract: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character, one network trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) makes every decision of a run, in combat and outside it. At the highest difficulty, Ascension 10, on two versions of the game current in November 2026 and on test seeds not played in training, AlphaDefect wins 62-77% of runs across six characters with greedy play and 68-80% with test-time search, after 1.3 to 6.7 billion decisions of training per character; runs uploaded by human players of all levels are won 11-20% of the time at the same difficulty. The networks read the game as entity records that identify each card, relic and enemy through a learned embedding and attributes from the game data, together with consequences of public information computed by the engine. Ablations show how much the agent depends on this encoding: without these identities, the network did not win a single run, and without the computed consequences it won 8.3 points fewer. To our knowledge, AlphaDefect is the strongest publicly reported STS2 agent as of November 2026.

infographic.key_insight: AlphaDefect reports expert-level Slay the Spire 2 performance using one PPO-trained network per character to make every decision throughout a run.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results highlight the importance of structured entity representations and engine-computed consequences for reinforcement learning in complex, stochastic environments.
method: Train one proximal policy optimization (PPO) network per character for combat and noncombat decisions.
Encode cards, relics and enemies using learned identity embeddings, game attributes and engine-computed public-information consequences.
Evaluate greedy play and test-time search on seeds excluded from training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 62–77% greedy and 68–80% search-assisted win rates across six characters at Ascension 10 on two game versions, after 1.3–6.7 billion training decisions per character, versus 11–20% for uploaded human runs.
infographic.watch_item: The uploaded human runs are not an expert-matched baseline, and reliance on game-engine features may complicate transfer to other environments.
infographic.paper_title: AlphaDefect: Expert-Level AI for Slay the Spire 2

title: ComputeWise: Measuring and Fixing GPU Waste by AI Research Agents
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Nina Pakhomova, Anurag Koul, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
abstract: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.

infographic.key_insight: ComputeWise finds that unaided AI research agents spend only 52% of GPU time on necessary work, while its harness removes over 80% of extra time to the answer across five models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Improving experiment orchestration can reduce costly GPU waste that utilization metrics alone fail to reveal.
method: Benchmark agents on research tasks using a simulated GPU that replays recorded runs.
Measure necessary computation, unnecessary computation, and idle time.
Combine prompting with deterministic orchestration code to reduce waste.
infographic.evidence_signal: Hundreds of simulated experiments found 52% necessary work, 22% unnecessary work, and 26% idle time; simple speed prompts, utilization prompts, and a job scheduler did not fix the waste.
infographic.watch_item: Replay-based simulation enables broad testing, but savings on real GPUs and workloads beyond the benchmark require validation.
infographic.paper_title: ComputeWise: Measuring and Fixing GPU Waste by AI Research Agents

title: Boltz-Flow: Generating High-Quality Robot Action from Boltzmann Machine
authors: Hengzhi Jiang, Haixu Liu, Jindou Jia, Tinglan Wang, Shaobo Chen, Yiren Zhao
abstract: Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves $π_{0.5}$ across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.

infographic.key_insight: Boltz-Flow improves robot action generation by replacing fixed Gaussian initialization with an observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base vision-language-action policy unchanged.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets richer, coordinated action initialization without redesigning the underlying flow-matching policy.
method: Use a conditional Boltzmann machine to assign energies to binary source states.
Train with an offline-demonstration-based listwise objective that aligns energy with action quality after frozen flow integration.
Solve the resulting Ising instance, decode its solution into continuous noise, and perform one standard flow integration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three benchmarks, Boltz-Flow improves π₀.₅, outperforms compared policy baselines and noise-optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, and ranks second to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus.
infographic.watch_item: Training uses a physical coherent Ising machine; hardware accessibility and Ising-solver latency warrant assessment before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Boltz-Flow: Generating High-Quality Robot Action from Boltzmann Machine

title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech
authors: Tianyi Huang, Lucas Su, Fred Zhang, Andy Liang, Gordon Li
abstract: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. Measured planner latency constrains this path; a deterministic retail schema attains 31.7% RFES, compared with 32.0% for the complete policy. In a separate 30-task $τ$-Voice simulation, schema-derived candidates with cached text-to-speech (TTS) audio attain 21/30 task-level RFES. Eligible audio begins 1.51 seconds before the user-audio endpoint among the 22 tasks with early speech, or 1.11 seconds over all 30 tasks with zero for tasks without eligible early speech. Semantic veto and endpoint waiting each pass 16/30 tasks. Together, the studies demonstrate a controlled coverage-compatibility trade-off and schema-based pre-endpoint operation, making the supported public commitment an explicit unit of voice-agent control.

infographic.key_insight: SayWhen enables early speech by releasing a task-directed act shared across plausible continuation plans and vetoing playback if new transcripts invalidate it.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Voice agents can reduce response latency by controlling supported public commitments rather than simply predicting and speaking the most likely response.
method: Identify a shared task-directed act across typed continuation plans.
Control speech release with a persistent transcript-based veto.
Measure regret-free early speech (RFES): supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 72 branching prefixes, generated plans achieved 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret versus 8.2% and 0.068 for Matched Top-One; separately, schema-derived candidates with cached TTS achieved task-level RFES on 21/30 simulated voice tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Planner latency limits generated-plan deployment, while schema-based results rely on predefined structure and cached TTS in a small simulation.
infographic.paper_title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech

title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
authors: Ramraj Chandradevan, Sayontan Ghosh, Vinoth Selvendran
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.

infographic.key_insight: CO-GRAFT shows that RL gains in search agents depend more on reasoning, search decisions, and answer extraction than query generation, which contributes at most 15% of the total gain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Role-level attribution can help engineers target agent improvements rather than assume better search queries drive higher accuracy.
method: Combine RL-trained and pre-RL policies in one live-retrieval trajectory, assigning each of four functional roles to one policy.
Evaluate all 16 role assignments without changing weights or retraining.
Use Shapley values to allocate RL gains and Möbius terms to quantify role interactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations span Search-R1 agents using Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2, two model sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO, and NQ and HotpotQA, with RL gains up to 32 exact-match points.
infographic.watch_item: Attributions depend on checkpoint characteristics and task-level search budgets; evaluating all 16 assignments also adds live-retrieval evaluation cost.
infographic.paper_title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting

title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
authors: Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Zechen Bai, Wenzheng Zeng, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yiqi Lin
abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

infographic.key_insight: Robot reliability depends strongly on the robot-use interface: effective designs reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Treat action abstraction and interaction design as core engineering choices, not merely wrappers around an embodied model.
method: Introduce RUIBench: 30 manipulation tasks across five suites.
Build RUIKit: 13 interfaces crossing six action abstractions with two interaction forms.
Compare interfaces under shared perception and control in simulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Changing only the interface shifted success rates from 45% to 81% for a frontier agent and from 13% to 47% for a fine-tuned 4B model.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation results do not establish real-world reliability, and agents frequently declared success despite observable failures, highlighting the need for task-level verification.
infographic.paper_title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?

title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
authors: Tianrun Gou, Qingyao Yang, Wendong Xu, Liang Chen, Kuan Li, Ngai Wong
abstract: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents can infer hidden circuit behavior from pin-level experiments, but fully correct and efficient reconstructions remain rare.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ChiProgramBench tests whether AI agents can turn experimental observations into cycle-accurate gate-level replacements while meeting power, delay, and area goals.
method: Probe 18 hidden, stateful circuits through simulated input and output pins.
Compare black-box discovery with function-guided reconstruction that adds circuit purpose and pin roles.
Submit netlists using public library cells; award efficiency credit only after all hidden functional tests pass.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 432 trials of six agent configurations, full-pass rates were 12.0% for black-box and 14.8% for function-guided tasks; only three of 58 fully passing designs improved combined power, area, and delay over the reference.
infographic.watch_item: Higher partial functional scores do not establish cycle-accurate correctness or efficient implementation.
infographic.paper_title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?

title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning
authors: Qianyi Chen, Bo Li
abstract: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.

infographic.key_insight: Tail-CRC separates budget-limited answer generation from abstention, using a single rollout to control expected wrong submissions under exchangeability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Teams can adjust submission-risk targets through recalibration rather than retraining, without paying for multiple inference samples.
method: Adapt the solver to forced termination using binary correctness rewards, then freeze it.
Score uncertainty using upper-tail token surprise within the generated answer.
Apply conformal risk control to decide whether to submit or abstain.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two Qwen models, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improved correct-submission rates by 15.0–29.6 percentage points on DAPO and 4.3–12.8 points on Omni-MATH; target-domain calibration reduced 8B Omni-MATH wrong submissions from 30.3% to 5.8% at 4K.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee controls expected wrong submissions, not error among submitted answers, and depends on exchangeability between calibration and deployment data.
infographic.paper_title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning

title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization
authors: Adeep Hande, Shaghayegh Agah, Neeraj Sharma, Karina Halevy, Sardar Hamidian
abstract: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-generated interactions can improve long-tail recommendation accuracy and coverage while constraining overall accuracy loss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can tune augmentation by item-popularity group to better serve sparse-data items without sacrificing overall recommendation quality beyond a chosen tolerance.
method: Partition items into groups by interaction frequency.
Optimize group-specific LLM augmentation for NDCG@20 and coverage, subject to an overall NDCG@20 degradation limit.
Test combined group strategies and ablate LLM scale and contextual richness under token constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: SASRec experiments report group-specific NDCG@20 gains exceeding 100% and 60% for extreme and regular long-tail items on an industrial dataset, and 40% and 25% on MovieLens-32M, with increased coverage and no significant overall degradation.
infographic.watch_item: Individually optimal group strategies are not simply additive, and richer augmentation context increases cost, requiring joint tuning and budget-aware validation.
infographic.paper_title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization

title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Mathijs A. Langezaal, Egon L. van den Broek, Lukas P. A. Arts, Marcel Goldberg, Grégoire Rey, Melissa C. Friesen
abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

infographic.key_insight: OPERAG combines retrieval with large language models to code free-text job descriptions without expert-labelled training databases, supporting large-scale occupational exposure assessment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Retrieving classification-specific coding information offers a flexible alternative to supervised tools restricted to occupational classifications seen during training.
method: Retrieve relevant occupational coding index information.
Combine retrieved information with LLM-based occupational classification.
Link occupational codes to Job Exposure Matrices for exposure assessment.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 36,062 AsiaLymph job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% fourth-level coding accuracy and 89.9–98.6% exposure-assessment accuracy using ALOHA+ and SHOCK.
infographic.watch_item: Fourth-level coding accuracy remained below the reported 51–56% human inter-coder reliability, and validation on one cohort does not establish universal generalization.
infographic.paper_title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation

title: Grower-in-the-loop AI for Deployable Precision Fertilisation in Sustainable Agriculture
authors: Xulong Wang, Yu Zhang, Gaoshan Bi, Menghui Zhou, Simon Jeffery, Max Davis
abstract: In agriculture, typically over half of the applied nitrogen fertiliser is lost to water and to air. Precision fertilisation aims to reduce these losses while maintaining yield and quality, yet existing tools struggle to capture farm-specific challenges in determining optimal nitrogen rates. Static recommendations are common and overlook on-farm constraints, such as delays due to weather or machinery availability, or change in budgets. Each constraint governs when and how growers apply fertiliser in practice. Here we present a grower-in-the-loop framework for winter wheat in England, combining baseline fertilisation planning from a machine learning-derived nitrogen-response curve with in-season adaptation via a large language model. We evaluated the framework using data from long-term experiments (LTEs), replicated field trials, and farm deployments. Retrospective model validation using LTEs confirmed low economic decision-loss across multiple seasons. Using field and farm trials, baseline schedules were shown to match standard-practice yields with less nitrogen, whereas in-season adjusted schedules additionally retained grain quality standards. Given this enhanced performance, in-season adaptation absorbed weather, machinery and budget constraints to keep recommendations executable. The framework therefore shows promise for translating static recommendations into adaptable, grower-informed decisions for sustainable fertiliser management.

infographic.key_insight: Combining machine learning-based nitrogen planning with grower-informed, in-season AI adaptation can reduce fertiliser use while maintaining winter wheat yield and grain quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Deployable decision-support systems need to adapt recommendations to weather, machinery availability and budget constraints, not just optimise fertiliser rates.
method: Derive baseline fertilisation plans from a machine learning-based nitrogen-response curve.
Use a large language model to adjust schedules during the season.
Incorporate grower input and operational constraints to keep recommendations executable.
infographic.evidence_signal: Long-term experiments showed low retrospective economic decision-loss; field trials and farm deployments matched standard-practice yields with less nitrogen, with adapted schedules also retaining grain quality standards.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence focuses on winter wheat in England; transferability to other crops and regions requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Grower-in-the-loop AI for Deployable Precision Fertilisation in Sustainable Agriculture

title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
authors: Yitong Qiao, Lei Liu, Yue Shen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu, Zhixuan Chu
abstract: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states from screenshots and execute mouse-and-keyboard actions, as well as a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data. The environment verifies both final answers and required clinical actions, and supports parallel trajectory collection for training. Benchmarking twelve vision-language models shows that current agents struggle across diverse clinical workflows, and simply increasing reasoning effort fails to yield consistent gains. Furthermore, MedUIGym supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards. After training, both Qwen3.5 models perform better on in-domain clinical tasks and generalize to tasks from external sources. By unifying tasks from existing benchmarks, dual-interface evaluation, and GUI trajectory collection, MedUIGym provides a testbed for studying how vision-language agents complete clinical tasks through the EHR's graphical interface. Our project page is available at https://github.com/yitong-qiao/MedUIGym.

infographic.key_insight: MedUIGym enables training and evaluation of clinical GUI agents, revealing persistent workflow difficulties while showing gains from task-based training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its paired GUI and native-tool interfaces over identical clinical data support comparisons of interface-dependent agent performance.
method: Unify 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families.
Run agents through screenshot observations and mouse-and-keyboard actions, verifying answers and required clinical actions.
Collect parallel GUI trajectories for offline learning and support online reinforcement learning from task rewards.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation of 12 vision-language models found inconsistent gains from increased reasoning effort; both trained Qwen3.5 models improved on in-domain tasks and generalized to external-source tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark improvements do not establish safety or reliability in live clinical EHR deployments.
infographic.paper_title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
